title: Becoming Boston: Eight Moments in the Geography of a Changing City
description: [Central Library in Copley Square] Note: This exhibition is held in the Leventhal Map and Education Gallery which is open Tuesday 11am-5pm, Wednesday 1pm-7pm, Thursday - Saturday 11am - 5pm, Sunday 1pm - 5pm. Please check their website for the most up to date hours and schedule.Maps trace out the complicated history of places, and we can use them to document geography in much the same way that we can use diaries and letters to document biography. In the eight cases of this exhibition, we follow the changing spatial forms of the place we now call Boston—from before the landscape carried that name all the way through the struggles, clashes, and dreams that continue to reshape the city today. These maps don’t merely depict facts about how the city looked at different moments in its history. Instead, they invite us to contemplate how geographic forces, both natural and human, have constructed the physical and social world around us, through large and small transformations that have transpired over many centuries. The Leventhal Map & Education Center regularly mounts exhibitions in our gallery, located in the historic McKim Building in the Boston Public Library in Copley Square. All of our exhibitions feature scholarly research as well as activities for families, children, and educators. Our permanent exhibit, Becoming Boston: Eight Moments in the Geography of a Changing City, is available any time our public gallery is open. Visit the digital exhibition to Becoming Boston here. title: Declarations: Printing a New Nation
description: [Central Library in Copley Square] Note: This exhibition is held in the Leventhal Map and Education Gallery which is open Tuesday 11am-5pm, Wednesday 1pm-7pm, Thursday - Saturday 11am - 5pm, Sunday 1pm - 5pm. Please check their website for the most up to date hours and schedule. On July 4, 1776, the Continental Congress ratified the Declaration of Independence in Philadelphia. The next day, the first printed copies were sent off and began to circulate throughout the thirteen colonies, which were now, on paper, independent states. Throughout July and August of 1776, the Declaration was reprinted in major American cities and small towns alike. Some of these new printings appeared in newspapers. Others were issued as large, single-sheet publications known as broadsides. Many versions, in both formats, were printed before the delegates to the Continental Congress began to sign the official handwritten Declaration in early August. These early printings of the Declaration were created at a time when the independence of the future United States was anything but certain. From the perspective of those who read it in the summer of 1776, we can see the Declaration of Independence in its original form: not yet a famous founding document, but breaking news. In the exhibition Declarations: Printing a New Nation, see eight different original printings of the Declaration of Independence, and take a journey that explores how the news of independence spread out from Philadelphia in the summer of 1776 when the ink was not yet dry on the founding documents of a new nation. description: [Central Library in Copley Square] On-going display in the Special Collections LobbyMonday - Friday, 9:30 a.m. - 4:30 p.m. Out of the Box: Unpacking the World of Archives opens up archives to visitors, demonstrating what archives are, what we can learn from them, and what archivists do to care for and make collections accessible. title: Lexicon
description: [Central Library in Copley Square] July 2026Aluminum · 18 × 18 × 2 ftAlfonso Parra Rubio · Erik StrandMIT Center for Bits and Atoms Lexicon is a free-form structural shell built from individual origami-folded cells assembled into a two-sided lattice, or interlocking framework. The folding and assembling process creates a structure that is as strong and rigid as typical building methods, but it is much lighter. The structure is made for this space, Deferrari Hall. Its light, curved shape contrasts with the Boylston Street Building's heavy and blocky brutalist architecture. Lexicon's three pointed shape is a reference to Rafael Guastavino's tiled ceilings in the Central Library's McKim Building. By bringing together influences from both of the Central Library's buildings, Lexicon celebrates the role of geometry in design and construction. A collaboration between the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), the Boston Public Library (BPL), and the Mayor's Office of Arts and Culture (MOAC). With Riccardo Foschi (University of Bologna), Rupert Malec (University of Innsbruck), Tomohiro Tachi (University of Tokyo), and Neil Gershenfeld (MIT Center for Bits and Atoms). Made possible and funded by MOAC.

title: Civic Engagement & Democracy: Library Science Meets Political Science
description: [Central Library in Copley Square] The Boston Public Library presents a unique panel on Civic Engagement, Political Science and the Role of the Library in Society. This panel, a public conversation, is presented adjacent to the American Political Science Association meeting in Boston September 3-6: https://connect.apsanet.org/ap.... BPL President David Leonard hosts an esteemed group of experts to discuss topics in civic engagement and libraries. This program will be recorded for viewing later and will be accessible on the BPL's YouTube channel: Boston Public Library - YouTube Speakers: Henry Brady (Berkeley) — What Is Civic Engagement? A Perspective from Political Science Kay L. Schlozman (Boston College) — What Explains Civic Engagement? The Critical Role of Education Donald Green (Columbia) — Voting as a Form of Civic Engagement and the Role of Voter Turnout in a Functioning Democracy Christina Wolbrecht (Notre Dame) — Civic engagement among young people and group differences in civic engagement along such fault lines of gender and race Laura Saunders (Simmons) and David Leonard (BPL) — The Centrality of Civic Engagement in the Public Library – History and Present-Day Opportunity. title: Everyone Wants a Long Life. Nobody Wants to Get Old.
description: [Central Library in Copley Square] Join us for this afternoon in-person talk in partnership with the Boston Village. Advances in medicine and public health have culminated in people rightly expecting to have a long life. And yet, we almost universally don't want to "get old." Here in the United States, being "old" is associated with decline in function, abilities, connection, independence and, ultimately, with loss of relevance and worth. Join us as Marie Clouqueur guides us to the possibility of maintaining our value and dignity in older age, even with limitations and loss. Drawing on her clinical work in geriatric psychiatry as well as examples in history and literature, Clouqueur will invite us to see older adults as protagonists who can drive the next advancements of our society. About the speaker: Marie Clouqueur, LICSW, is a clinical social worker at McLean Hospital specializing in older adults and family work. She founded and leads the dementia support program in the Division of Geriatric Psychiatry. Her clinical work provides group and individual psychotherapy to improve caregiver resilience and to support people living with dementia. Marie Clouqueur is speaking as a part of Boston Village's 25th Anniversary Speaker Series titled Aging in Place: Living Your Best Life @ Home. title: Exhibition: Life, Liberty, and the Pursuit of Happiness
description: [Central Library in Copley Square] To mark the 250th anniversary of the signing of the Declaration of Independence, the Boston Public Library's Community History Department partnered with Revolutionary Spaces to offer a free and public program series called "Life, Liberty, and the Pursuit of Happiness." Named for the unalienable rights identified in the Declaration—rights that inherently belong to all human beings, and that governments are created to protect—these programs brought people together to explore, question, and find inspiration in the Declaration of Independence. During two printmaking workshops and four declaration writing workshops at the BPL, library visitors reflected on the 250th anniversary of the American Revolution. Displayed together, the art prints and writing pieces made by community members speak to the ongoing American struggle to create and sustain a free society. As a viewer of the exhibition, we invite you to consider: How do I identify with this nation's founding document? What do I celebrate? How do I use my voice in protest? About Community History The BPL Community History Department aims to democratize the expression of history by supporting people in their efforts to document the stories of themselves and their communities. We offer resources, programs, and support for local and community history work based on people’s lived experiences, knowledge, and expertise. About Revolutionary Spaces Revolutionary Spaces stewards the historic Old South Meeting House and Old State House as landmarks, museums, and active civic spaces. Its mission is to bring people together to explore the American struggle to create and sustain a free society—using history as a powerful tool for civic engagement and public dialogue. For more information, visit RevolutionarySpaces.org or follow them on social media at @RevSpaces. Accessibility Notice: We strive to make our events accessible. title: Author Talk: Emily Sweeney - Dropkick Murphy : A Legendary Life
description: [Central Library in Copley Square] Join Boston Globe reporter Emily Sweeney with her authentic Boston accent, for a discussion of her biography of local luminary Dr. John Murphy, aka "Dropkick" Murphy and his life in and outside the wrestling arena. Newspapers called him the “the man with the cast-iron toes,” “the best drop-kicker in wrestling,” and “one of the mat game’s biggest box office attractions.” But Dr. John “Dropkick” Murphy’s legacy extends far beyond the wrestling ring. Decades before the Betty Ford Center became a household name — and long before the band the Dropkick Murphys named themselves in his honor — the phrase going to Dropkick’s meant a person struggling with addiction needed help and would soon get some. This book chronicles for the first time the unbelievable life of Dr. “Dropkick” Murphy, a professional wrestler who put himself through medical school during the Great Depression and then opened Bellows Farm in Acton, MA, a one-of-a-kind institution that served as both a facility where elite athletes could train as well as a secluded place where down-on-their-luck alcoholics could go to sober up discreetly. The celebrities who frequented Dropkick Murphy’s farm were many, and numerous professional athletes would go there to focus on their training and work out in his state-of-the-art gymnasium. As a result, Bellows Farm featured an unrivaled and revolving cast of colorful characters who brought it to life. Drawing on years of research and interviews, author Emily Sweeney goes behind the scenes to reveal the untold story of Murphy’s life, his farm, and the legendary events that unfolded there. Emily Sweeney is a staff reporter at the Boston Globe and author of the books Boston Organized Crime and Gangland Boston. The people who tend The Loom are out of options. Something has reached across the threshold looking for help. It chose you. In this two-hour role-playing game, you'll battle giant moths and monsters, solve puzzles, and work together with your group to help save the people of The Loom. title: 42nd Annual Boston Film Festival: Papertown (Film Screening & Discussion)
description: [Central Library in Copley Square] Join us for a screening of the feature-length documentary Papertown as a part of the 2026 Boston Film Festival. The film will be followed by a Q&A with Executive Producer Ryan Suffern. We'll begin the afternoon with a screening of the 13 minute documentary clip, The Kid From Boston. Papertown is a feature-length documentary centered on the closure of the Canton paper mill and the profound ripple effects felt across Haywood County and Western North Carolina. At its heart, the film is not about the loss of a single industry, but about what happens when identity, labor, land, and community are forced to reimagine themselves at a moment of transition. This film emerges from within the region it portrays. It is grounded in lived experience, long-term relationships, and a deep respect for the people whose stories are often reduced to headlines or economic data. Papertown offers a human, nuanced portrait of a community at a crossroads — and in doing so, creates space for reflection, dialogue, and possibility. We are incredibly excited to have Grammy-award winning musician Dave Matthews join us as an Executive Producer recently. Even more, we are excited about the song he wrote especially for the film, accompanied by alternative country artist, Sierra Ferrell. We feel it is the perfect ending to the film. -- from the New Union Films website.The Kid From Boston is a feature documentary about Terrence Clarke, a Boston basketball prodigy whose talent and infectious personality made him one of the most beloved prospects ever to emerge from the city.After starring at Brewster Academy and the University of Kentucky, his path to the NBA seemed inevitable. But just weeks before the 2021 Draft, a tragic car accident took his life.Told through the voices of his family, coaches, and teammates, the film celebrates Terrence’s life, legacy, and the city that shaped him.FilmmakerAlex Stoddard is a filmmaker, platinum-certified music producer, and former college basketball player from Wellesley, Massachusetts. His production credits include SoulFly and the gold-certified single ‘OMDB’. His latest documentary, The Kid From Boston, tells the story of Terrence Clarke, a Boston basketball phenom and Alex’s former AAU teammate. More information about the Boston Film Festival can be found here: The Boston Film Festival Registration requested and seating is first come, first served. Doors will open to the public by 1:15 pm. title: Lowell Lecture Series: Sarah Botstein, Co-Director of The American Revolution from Florentine Films
description: [Central Library in Copley Square] Join us in person or over Zoom Webinar as the Boston Public Library welcomes Sarah Botstein as a speaker for the Lowell Lecture Series. As a filmmaker who has worked closely with Ken Burns for over 30 years as a part of Florentine Films, Sarah will talk about her latest film, PBS's The American Revolution, historical filmmaking, and the revolutionary techniques that Florentine Films uses to bring history to life. Botstein will be in conversation with Imari Paris Jeffries from Embrace Boston and the program will be introduced by BPL President David Leonard. After the main program, in-person audience members can meet the speaker in the Connector Space located just outside of Rabb Hall. This program will happen in-person and over Zoom Webinar. We plan to open doors twenty minutes in advance for our in-person audience. Sarah Botstein has worked with Ken Burns for nearly 30 years and produced some of his most popular and acclaimed documentaries on PBS. Most recently, she produced and co-directed The American Revolution. Her previous work includes The U.S. and the Holocaust, Hemingway, College Behind Bars, The Vietnam War, Prohibition, The War, and Jazz. Botstein also works closely with PBS LearningMedia to develop educational materials as part of the Ken Burns Classroom, and she was an original contributor to Ken Burns's UNUM. Botstein is now working on a three-part series about Lyndon B. Johnson and the Great Society. Sarah Botstein is joined by Imari Paris Jeffries, CEO of Embrace Boston. Imari Paris Jeffries , Ph.D., is President and CEO of Embrace, an arts, culture, and community organization reshaping public memory as public policy and advancing belonging through justice. His work begins with a simple premise: cities are shaped not only by policy and economics, but by story, monument, silence, and who is remembered. Under his leadership, Embrace has grown into a civic force committed to centering Black life in public space. The Embrace Monument on Boston Common honoring Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. and Coretta Scott King stands as a declaration that love, struggle, and Black life belong at the heart of the city's landscape. What began as a monument has evolved into a movement, paired with institutional commitments designed to shift culture in lasting ways. Beyond this first monument, Imari has advanced collaboration on the WEB Du Bois Monument and a forthcoming national arts and civic center in Downtown Crossing, envisioned as a twenty-first century civic home where culture and democracy meet. Before leading Embrace, Imari served in executive leadership roles at Parenting Journey, the Italian Home for Children, Jumpstart, Boston Rising, and Friends of the Children Boston, consistently strengthening governance, stabilizing finances, and embedding equity as an operational discipline. A dedicated civic leader, Imari serves as a Trustee of the University of Massachusetts System and on the boards of Boston Ballet and GBH. He has been recognized among Boston Magazine's 100 Most Influential Bostonians and is a recipient of the Mel King Social Innovator Award. A four-time graduate of UMass Boston, and a United States Army veteran, he lives in Boston with his family This program is produced in partnership with GBH and PBS. This program is part of the Lowell Lecture Series generously sponsored by the Lowell Institute through the Boston Public Library Fund. Accessibility Notice: We strive to make our events accessible. title: Music Production with Hamstank: Beats, Recording, Mixing, & Mastering [#teencentral]
description: [Central Library in Copley Square] Are you totally new to creating music but curious to try your hand? Maybe you are an experienced music artist ready to take your talent to the next level? Wherever you are in your music journey, come to the Lab at Teen Central on Friday afternoons. We are fully equipped for your digital music creation needs with: Audio booth with studio quality Neuman microphone & Apogee Duet audio interfaceiMac computers with Logic Pro & GarageBandAlienware computers with Ableton LiveBlue Yeti microphonesStudio quality headphonesAlesis V25 MIDI KeyboardsLaunchpad MIDI Controller And on Fridays you will be accompanied in your journey by Hamstank, our resident music producer! He’ll meet you wherever you are and get you: Making beatsRecordingWriting songsMixing & mastering Registration is available but not required. Tony “Hamstank” Hamoui is a professional music producer and educator based out of the Greater Boston area. With the goal of positively shaping culture, Hamstank is driven to study, teach, and experiment with the art and science of sound, one track at a time. As a Boston-bred music producer, Hamstank works with artists to fulfill their creative vision. Hamstank has worked with artists such as Cliff Notez, Oompa, VQnC, Still Electric, Fire and the Field, among many others. Hamstank runs Stank Factory Recordings, a Somerville-based music production studio. The Lab at Teen Central is the teen-exclusive digital makerspace at Central Library in Copley Square. This space contains high performing iMacs and Alienware PCs — all equipped with the Adobe Creative Cloud and other creative software — as well as 3D printers, an audio booth, sewing machines, Cricut cutting machines, and more! The Lab is open to all 6th-12th graders (12-17 year-olds) who are interested in getting creative with technology. It is a resource for the teens of Boston to explore new technology, gain 21st century skills, express themselves creatively, and become better digital citizens. Accessibility Notice: We strive to make our events accessible. To request a disability accommodation and/or language services, contact bskywall@bpl.org. title: Author Talk: N.K. Jemisin on Revolutionary Ideas in Fantasy Fiction
description: [Central Library in Copley Square] In-person registration is full with a waitlist. Please register to attend virtually HERE. Noted and award-winning fantasy fiction author N.K. Jemisin discusses her work and her 20-plus-year career that has been inspired by revolutionary ideas. N. K. Jemisin is a fantasy author and 2020 MacArthur Fellow. Since beginning her professional career in the early 2000s, her short fiction and novels have been recognized with multiple Hugo, Nebula, and Locus Awards. Most of her works have been optioned for television or film, and collectively her novels, including the Broken Earth trilogy, have sold over two million copies. After twenty years working in higher education as an applied counseling psychologist, she “retired” in 2016 to become a full-time writer, writing instructor, and public speaker. Her speculative works range widely in theme, though with repeated motifs: resistance and oppression, loneliness and belonging, and Wouldn’t It Be Cool If This One Ridiculous Thing Happened. In her spare time she’s into tabletop and video games, biking, fanfiction, and urban gardening. She lives in Brooklyn with her son and two cats. After the talk, N.K. Jemisin will sign copies of her books with our local bookstore partner, Trident Booksellers. Accessibility Notice: We strive to make our events accessible. title: AI Safety Awareness Project: Where's AI in 2026 and Where is it Going?
description: [Central Library in Copley Square] A community meeting and information session about the future of AI hosted by the AI Safety Awareness Project​. This is a free, public workshop with no technical background needed. ​For the last several years, AI systems have advanced at a pace that has stunned the public and even surprised leading experts. These systems are reshaping work, the economy, relationships, and even crime extremely quickly.​This workshop will explore where AI may be in the next 1-5 years and what that means for daily life for all of us. We’ll tackle urgent and important questions like:Jobs: Could AI lead to mass unemployment or will it help create entirely new kinds of work?Crime: How might AI supercharge scams, hacking, and even crime?Companions: Will people form deep emotional bonds or even romantic relationships with AI companions?Society: How do top researchers think these trends will shape our future?​What participants will get:​A fast-paced, beginner-friendly overview of today’s most powerful AI systemsLive demos that reveal both the breakthroughs and the riskInteractive forecasting exercises where you’ll test your predictions about AI’s impact against the broader community​Come ready to explore a future arriving faster than most people realize. A future that could transform not just how we work, but how we trust, connect, and even love.Accessibility Notice: We strive to make our events accessible. description: [Central Library in Copley Square] In-person AND online registration seats are full. Registration and the waitlist are closed. Join the Boston Public Library and the Boston Public Library Fund as Author Ann Patchett headlines the 2026 Maury A. Bromsen Lecture. Ann Patchett has been the recipient of numerous awards, including a National Humanities Medal and the PEN/Faulkner Award. Her novel, The Dutch House, was a finalist for the Pulitzer Prize. She was named one of TIME’s 100 Most Influential People in the World and is a member of the American Academy of Arts and Letters. Her books have been both New York Times Notable Books and New York Times bestsellers, and her work has been translated into more than thirty languages. The Maury A. Bromsen Lecture Series at the Boston Public Library was established to celebrate authors whose work illuminates the depth, dignity, and complexity of the human experience. In its renewed form, the series will foreground literature that brings individual lives fully into view—work that reflects Maury Bromsen’s vision of humanistic bibliography by exploring how personal narratives, lived experience, and moral imagination shape our collective understanding of history, culture, and community. The lecture offers a space for distinguished writers to reflect on their creative journeys, share insights into their recent work, and consider how storytelling can deepen empathy and understanding in a complex world. title: Banned in Boston: Is Censorship Still Stifling Free Speech? (A Talks for Better Living Event)
description: [Central Library in Copley Square] Join us in partnership with the Citywide Friends of the Boston Public Library for a timely and thought-provoking conversation featuring New York Law School Professor of Law Emerita Nadine Strossen and Harvard Law School Professor Randall Kennedy —two of America's foremost authorities on free expression and the First Amendment. Why is some speech still banned not only in Boston, but also around the United States? What lines does the First Amendment draw between permissible and impermissible speech restrictions? Should those lines be redrawn in light of new technologies and their associated new dangers? Launching Banned Books Week, this engaging discussion will explore a topic that is as timeless as it is timely: the tension between free speech and censorship. From book bans and social media bans, to “cancel culture,” to multiple federal measures that many judges have struck down as violating the First Amendment, free speech is facing threats from all across the ideological spectrum. Our distinguished panelists will tackle the issues shaping today's public debate, including: What speech the First Amendment actually protects – and does not protect – in contrast with widespread misunderstandings on point.Why the Supreme Court Justices, all across the ideological spectrum, strongly protect speech that is deeply unpopular in the general public, including “hate speech,” “extremist speech,” and “disinformation.”What history teaches us about the dangers of powerful new communications technologies –– and the dangers of censoring them.How each of us can help foster a culture of open dialogue, intellectual curiosity, and democratic resilience. For everyone who cares deeply about civil liberties, loves books, enjoys spirited debate, or simply wants to better understand one of the defining issues of our time, this is a conversation you will not want to miss. Come prepared to be challenged. Come curious. Leave with a deeper understanding of why free speech matters to everyone. About the speakers: Nadine Strossen: New York Law School Professor Emerita and Senior Fellow at FIRE (the Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression), was President of the American Civil Liberties Union from 1991 to 2008. An internationally acclaimed free speech scholar and advocate, who regularly addresses diverse audiences and provides media commentary around the world, Strossen serves on the advisory boards of the ACLU and several academic freedom/freespeech organizations. She is the Host and Project Consultant for Free To Speak, a 3-hour documentary film series distributed on public television in 2023.Randall Kennedy is Michael R. Klein Professor at Harvard Law School where he teaches courses on contracts, criminal law, and the regulation of race relations. He was born in Columbia, South Carolina. For his education he attended St. Albans School, Princeton University, Oxford University, and Yale Law School. He served as a law clerk for Judge J. Skelly Wright of the United States Court of Appeals and for Justice Thurgood Marshall of the United States Supreme Court. He is a member of the bar of the District of Columbia and the Supreme Court of the United States. Awarded the 1998 Robert F. Kennedy Book Award for Race, Crime, and the Law, Mr. Kennedy writes for a wide range of scholarly and general interest publications. His other books are For Discrimination: Race, Affirmative Action, and the Law (2013), The Persistence of the Color Line: Racial Politics and the Obama Presidency (2011), Sellout: The Politics of Racial Betrayal (2008), Interracial Intimacies: Sex, Marriage, Identity, and Adoption (2003), and Nigger: The Strange Career of a Troublesome Word (2002). A member of the American Law Institute, the American Academy of Arts and Sciences, and the American Philosophical Association, Mr. Kennedy is also a Trustee emeritus of Princeton University. title: Music Production with Hamstank: Beats, Recording, Mixing, & Mastering [#teencentral]
description: [Central Library in Copley Square] Are you totally new to creating music but curious to try your hand? Maybe you are an experienced music artist ready to take your talent to the next level? Wherever you are in your music journey, come to the Lab at Teen Central on Friday afternoons. We are fully equipped for your digital music creation needs with: Audio booth with studio quality Neuman microphone & Apogee Duet audio interfaceiMac computers with Logic Pro & GarageBandAlienware computers with Ableton LiveBlue Yeti microphonesStudio quality headphonesAlesis V25 MIDI KeyboardsLaunchpad MIDI Controller And on Fridays you will be accompanied in your journey by Hamstank, our resident music producer! He’ll meet you wherever you are and get you: Making beatsRecordingWriting songsMixing & mastering Registration is available but not required. Tony “Hamstank” Hamoui is a professional music producer and educator based out of the Greater Boston area. With the goal of positively shaping culture, Hamstank is driven to study, teach, and experiment with the art and science of sound, one track at a time. As a Boston-bred music producer, Hamstank works with artists to fulfill their creative vision. Hamstank has worked with artists such as Cliff Notez, Oompa, VQnC, Still Electric, Fire and the Field, among many others. Hamstank runs Stank Factory Recordings, a Somerville-based music production studio. The Lab at Teen Central is the teen-exclusive digital makerspace at Central Library in Copley Square. This space contains high performing iMacs and Alienware PCs — all equipped with the Adobe Creative Cloud and other creative software — as well as 3D printers, an audio booth, sewing machines, Cricut cutting machines, and more! The Lab is open to all 6th-12th graders (12-17 year-olds) who are interested in getting creative with technology. It is a resource for the teens of Boston to explore new technology, gain 21st century skills, express themselves creatively, and become better digital citizens. description: [Central Library in Copley Square] The Boston Research Center (BRC) is a digital community history and archives lab that supports Boston residents in telling the stories of their neighborhoods and communities. How We Can Help: The Boston Research Center helps bring Boston’s deep neighborhood and community histories to light through the creation and use of new technologies. The BRC can support your ideas and projects in many different ways. This support may look like: Offering free introductory workshops about digital humanities tools and methodsSharing resources and toolkits to help demystify digital projects and community history workConsulting on project design and maintenance Connecting community historians with subject experts, research resources, and grant opportunitiesProviding technical support for digital history projectsHelping promote events centered on community projects If you aren't sure what you need, drop in! title: Starting and Growing a Business: The SBA Advantage
description: [Central Library in Copley Square] Are you thinking of starting a business? Do you need small business assistance? The U.S. Small Business Administration (SBA) can help! Join Shelly Gillis, Outreach and Marketing Specialist with the SBA in the Massachusetts District Office to learn how their programs and services can help your business. This workshop aims to provide you with a better understanding of the various programs and services offered by the SBA that are available to prospective or current entrepreneurs who need assistance in starting or expanding their businesses. We’ll cover: An overview of the SBA and its Resource Partner Network How the SBDC, CWE, VBOC and SCORE can help through business training and 1:1 mentoringAccessing capital SBA-backed loan programs Let the Small Business Administration (SBA), help you get “procurement-ready” to market your firm’s products and services to the Federal Government through our Resource Partners Network. Federal Government Contracting can represent a very profitable market for your business — but it can also be extremely complex to get started and thrive. The SBA and its resource partners can help you determine if your business is ready for federal contracting by assessing your business for: Marketability​Structure and experience​Systems and capacityAbility to find contracts Shelly Gillis is an Outreach and Marketing Specialist with the Small Business Administration Massachusetts District Office. She’s passionate about supporting small businesses and entrepreneurs in the Commonwealth by connecting them with community partners and resources. Formerly with for the US Census Bureau for 13 years, she was involved in both field operations and Decennial Census promotion in the Boston area. She has a background in sales and marketing, having worked as an award-winning sales representative and sales manager with Entertainment Publications in Massachusetts. Ms. Gillis holds a master’s degree in education from UMass Boston and a Bachelor of Journalism degree from the University of Nebraska with an advertising major. She is a proud Boston resident for 32 years, but loves her Nebraska roots and is a loyal Cornhusker fan. Accessibility Notice: We strive to make our events accessible. title: An In-Person Living Room Conversation — Trustworthy Elections (Local)
description: [Central Library in Copley Square] In Living Room Conversations, participants will take turns talking and listening to share and learn about the topic being discussed. Facilitated by library staff members, these conversations offer a simple, sociable, and structured way to practice communicating across differences while building understanding and relationships. About This Living Room Conversation Trust is a critical component of building and maintaining healthy families, communities, institutions, and countries. What happens when it starts to dwindle or is lost entirely? Trust is built over time. It can be challenged by people with different views or backgrounds as well as events that call into question the intent of our institutions and media. Increasingly, concerns about access to voting and election integrity have led to a questioning of election results. This conversation is designed to encourage reflection on key disconnects we are currently experiencing. What happens when we don’t trust our elections? title: Lowell Lecture: AI and Civic Engagement with Nathan Sanders, Dr. Avijit Ghosh, Jessica Chapel and David Leonard
description: [Central Library in Copley Square] Join us in person or over Zoom Webinar as the Boston Public Library welcomes AI experts Nathan Sanders, Dr. Avijit Ghosh, and Jessica Chapel as panelists for this conversation about AI and civic engagement as a part of the 2026 Lowell Lecture Series. This program will be moderated by BPL President David Leonard. Jessica Chapel is Chief of Digital & Online Services at Boston Public Library, where she leads digitization, digital stewardship, and UX, with a growing focus on AI's role in information access and discovery. Her department operates Digital Commonwealth, the statewide repository connecting 270+ Massachusetts libraries, archives, and museums. She co-hosts an ongoing speaker series with the Leventhal Map & Education Center on AI and cultural heritage collections, and co-moderates BPL's AI Interest Group. Dr. Avijit Ghosh is a Lead Technical AI Policy Researcher at Hugging Face 🤗, a central platform for open AI models, datasets, and research tools used by industry, government, and academic developers worldwide. He is also a Research Affiliate at the University of Connecticut. His work sits at the intersection of AI research and policy, with a central focus on how we measure and benchmark AI systems, and whether those measurements can actually be trusted. He founded and leads the EvalEval Coalition, a multi-stakeholder initiative bringing methodological rigor and accountability to AI evaluation. His broader research spans algorithmic bias, agent autonomy, AI for science, and third-party flaw disclosure, with coverage in The New York Times, Forbes, The Guardian, ProPublica, Wired, and MIT Technology Review. He represents Hugging Face in technical engagements with legislators and regulators in the United States, United Kingdom, European Union, and Singapore on open-source AI governance and evaluation standards. His work has helped shape AI regulation in New York City and prompted Facebook to remove its biased ad targeting algorithm. Nathan E. Sanders is a data scientist focused on making policymaking more participatory. His research spans machine learning, astrophysics, public health, environmental justice, and more. He has served in fellowships and the Massachusetts legislature and the Berkman-Klein Center at Harvard University. You can find his writing on AI and democracy in publications like The New York Times and The Atlantic and at his website, nsanders.me. After the main program, in-person audience members can meet the speakers in the Connector Space located just outside of Rabb Hall. This program will happen in-person and over Zoom Webinar. We plan to open doors twenty minutes in advance for our in-person audience. Please note: registration will open six weeks before the program date, on Wednesday September 9 at 6:00 pm. This program is part of the Lowell Lecture Series generously sponsored by the Lowell Institute through the Boston Public Library Fund. Accessibility Notice: We strive to make our events accessible. title: Author Talk: Courtney Humphries - Climate Change and the Future of Boston
description: [Central Library in Copley Square] Join us as author Courtney Humphries discusses her new book on the climate impacts facing Boston and the city’s efforts to mitigate and adapt to a changing climate.Like many of the world’s iconic coastal cities, Boston faces potentially severe impacts from climate change. Depending on global emissions, Boston could face several feet of sea level rise this century, which would leave many parts of the city subject to tidal and storm flooding. Precipitation events could become more frequent and extreme, and its already-humid summers could become dangerously hot, with most days over 90 degrees. Today, Boston is a booming city with a growing population, a glittering new waterfront neighborhood, world-class universities and a strong economy. Its future risks and opportunities related to climate change are shaped by the 400-year environmental, social and economic history of the city’s development. Climate Change and the Future of Boston describes how Boston’s history and current context shape future climate impacts and examines the mitigation and adaptation strategies the city has taken. Boston is a leader in acknowledging the problem of climate change; it has set a goal of becoming carbon neutral by 2050, among other climate-related goals. It has also developed science-based climate models and undertaken a robust planning process to identify strategies to protect its waterfront from flooding and increase its resilience to other climate-related impacts. Its mayor has embraced a progressive Green New Deal for Boston emphasizing the need for an inclusive and equitable approach to climate mitigation and adaptation. But the city also faces structural challenges, such as aging infrastructure, historic racial inequities, rising gentrification and income inequality and ongoing political and regulatory obstacles that hinder efforts to adapt in an efficient and just manner. She will conclude with a set of forward-looking scenarios about what the future may have in store for the city and the lessons it holds for other coastal cities struggling with these challenges.Courtney Humphries, PhD, is an interdisciplinary scholar, teacher, and award-winning journalist writing about science and the urban environment. title: Author Talk with Peggy Levitt—Move Over, Mona Lisa
description: [Central Library in Copley Square] Join us for an author talk and signing with Peggy Levitt, Wellesley College professor and renowned sociologist. In her new book, Move Over, Mona Lisa, Peggy asks: If the public is loudly calling for a wider range of art, literature, and ideas in our museums, libraries, and classrooms, why are our cultural and educational institutions so slow in making the change? Her answer is what she calls the "inequality pipeline," the layers of obstacles that keep art and ideas from circulating freely across the globe. Drawing on conversations with artists, writers, and cultural professionals in Argentina, Lebanon, and South Korea, Peggy shows that many of them have stopped waiting for old gatekeepers to change and are instead building new, alternative hubs and pathways that let art and ideas travel from cities like "Buenos Aires to Mexico City without having to pass through Madrid." Peggy takes us from the studios and desks where art and ideas are first created, through the museums and institutions that circulate and exhibit them, to the classrooms where they're researched and taught. Along the way, she reveals how cities, museums, and libraries influence more about both what creatives do and what the public learns than we might generally assume. The result is a hopeful, sharply observed new theory of how global cultural and intellectual change really happens. Peggy Levitt is the Mildred Lane Kemper Chair of Sociology at Wellesley College. She is also a co-founder of the Global (De)Centre. Her latest book, Move Over, Mona Lisa: Reimagining What We Read, Look At, and Learn was published this year by Stanford University Press. Peggy has previously written on social protections across borders, museums as site of immigration and national story-building, the influence of immigration on religion, and the socio-political realities of 1st and 2nd generation American immigrants. She co-directed the Transnational Studies Initiative and the Politics and Social Change Workshop at the Weatherhead Center for International Affairs at Harvard University and the Hauser Center for Nonprofit Organizations at the Harvard Kennedy School from 1998 to 2020. Peggy received Honorary Doctoral Degrees from the University of Helsinki (2017) and from Maastricht University (2014) and has held numerous fellowships and guest professorships at academic and research institutions from Edinburgh to Hong Kong.Accessibility Notice: We strive to make our events accessible. description: [Central Library in Copley Square] Save the date to join us in person or online over Zoom Webinar to hear author Nicholas Boggs speak about his recent bestselling biography of James Baldwin, Baldwin: A Love Story, in celebration of LGBTQ+ History Month! Registration will open on September 16th, 2026. After the hour-long talk, Nicholas Boggs will sign copies of Baldwin during a signing facilitated by our local, independent bookseller, Trident Booksellers. Nicholas Boggs is the author of the New York Times bestselling biography, Baldwin: A Love Story (FSG, 2025), winner of the National Book Critics Circle John Leonard Prize, the PEN/Jacqueline Bograd Weld Award for Biography, the Stonewall/Israel Fishman Nonfiction Award, and the Randy Shilts Nonfiction Award. title: Handwriting the Constitution
description: [Central Library in Copley Square] Patrons and visitors are invited to handwrite the U.S. Constitution in Bates Hall at the Central Library in Copley Square. This program aims to create time and a quiet space to reflect and deepen one's understanding of this historic document. All supplies will be provided. Participants will first stop by the supply table outside of Bates Hall to pick up writing supplies and a copy of the Constitution, before proceeding to Bates Hall. Reproductions of John Adams's personal copy of the Constitution held by Special Collections will also be available to transcribe. This program is self-paced. Patrons are invited to stay for the whole session or simply stay as long as they would like. About Handwriting the Constitution Handwriting the Constitution is a social art project begun in 2017 by artist Morgan O'Hara. It invites people from all walks of life to meet in public spaces to handwrite the U.S. Constitution or other documents written to protect human rights and freedoms. This art practice was created so that people will know their rights, deepen their understanding of laws created to protect these rights, and to help resist negative thinking. The goal of this art practice is to encourage people to hold their own Handwriting sessions on a recurring basis; to create a physical and psychological space that explores the practice of concentrated writing as an art form, and a process designed to bring people together in a quiet and calming way, all by focusing on human rights. It has been identified as a powerful and transformative form of activism for introverts. Accessibility Notice: We strive to make our events accessible. title: Author Talk: Linford D. Fisher — Stealing America: The Hidden Story of Indigenous Slavery in U.S. History
description: [Central Library in Copley Square] Join author Linford Fisher in a discussion of his book, Stealing America, where he shows that although the first enslaved Africans arrived in Jamestown in 1619, European slavery in America began more than a century before. The enslavement of Indigenous people began in the years just after 1492, ensnaring an estimated three to six million Natives throughout the Americas. Although largely erased from the public consciousness, Native enslavement continued for centuries to become a colossal phenomenon that affected nearly 600,000 Native Americans in North America alone, revealing the shocking truth that American colonizers enslaved Natives in roughly the same numbers as they imported enslaved Africans. From Virginia to California, from New England to Barbados, Stealing America traces the history of Indigenous enslavement and land dispossession, detailing how colonizers captured Natives and often deliberately mislabeled them as Black slaves to avoid detection. While the American Revolution pealed the bells of freedom for colonists, it paved a larcenous trail of westward expansion that subsequently plundered Indigenous land and stole the labor of Natives from nations like the Cherokee, Navajo, Nisean, and many others. “This double theft,” Fisher writes, “was central to the origins, growth, and eventual success of the English colonies and the United States—not just initially but throughout all of American history.” Fisher will weave together accounts of major episodes in American history including early colonization, the American Revolution, and the Civil War with lesser-known stories of Native enslavement and land loss. Fisher upends conventional histories about the nature of American slavery, revealing enslaved Natives in places we have overlooked, including southern antebellum plantations and the nineteenth-century American West. After Congress outlawed Native slavery in 1867, Americans forced Indigenous children into boarding schools and white homes, where they labored under forced assimilation. This practice was not reformed until the latter twentieth century, when Native nations finally secured increasing rights and self-determination. Linford D. Fisher is an associate professor of history at Brown University. The author of The Indian Great Awakening and principal investigator of the Stolen Relations project, he lives in Providence, Rhode Island. title: Intro to Copyright (Volunteer Lawyers for the Arts)
description: [Central Library in Copley Square] What is copyright? What does it do? Why have I been told to “copyright” my work? Do I “own” copyright? Why does this matter? Copyright is a fundamental legal protection that gives creators the power to control access to their work. In this workshop, we’ll explain basic principles of copyright: what it is, what it protects, what protection entails, and how you can be proactive in securing copyright protection for your own creative work. title: Boston Research Center Office Hours
description: [Central Library in Copley Square] The Boston Research Center (BRC) is a digital community history and archives lab that supports Boston residents in telling the stories of their neighborhoods and communities. Want help on your digital history project? Attend BRC Office Hours on the third Thursday of every month, in person at the BPL Central Library. BRC Office Hours are free and open to the public. No registration needed! Drop by the Mezzanine Conference Room 1 between 3 pm and 4:30 pm. How We Can Help: The Boston Research Center helps bring Boston’s deep neighborhood and community histories to light through the creation and use of new technologies. The BRC can support your ideas and projects in many different ways. This support may look like: Offering free introductory workshops about digital humanities tools and methodsSharing resources and toolkits to help demystify digital projects and community history workConsulting on project design and maintenance Connecting community historians with subject experts, research resources, and grant opportunitiesProviding technical support for digital history projectsHelping promote events centered on community projects If you aren't sure what you need, drop in! Our knowledgeable team members will be happy to assist you. Check out our projects to see our work. This program is organized by Boston Public Library's Community History Department. title: Author Talk: Paul Lewis — How Poe's "Raven" Became America's Most Famous Poem
description: [Central Library in Copley Square] Join Boston College Professor Emeritus Paul Lewis in a discussion of his new book on Edgar Allan Poe's famous poem. In 1845, over 5,300 poems were published in American magazines. Most immediately began their deserved descent into oblivion. Poe's "Raven" stands as the most conspicuous exception to this. But why? What factors influenced the attention devoted to "The Raven" from the day when it was first published? Why was it widely reprinted, praised, criticized, and mocked during the next weeks and months? Why did it inspire parodies that replaced Poe's "saintly bird of yore" with a veritable menagerie of other animals—including an owl, gazelle, turkey, pig, dog, cats, rats, and (eek!) bedbugs? And how did Poe's reputation—as a literary brawler and harsh book reviewer and as a man who struggled with money and alcohol—play into the reception of "The Raven"? Signed copies of Paul Lewis' Quothing "The Raven" The First Responses to America's Most Famous Poem will be available at this book-launch event. Paul Lewis is a Professor Emeritus at Boston College, a past president of the Poe Studies Association, and the curator of exhibitions on literary Boston. As the Board of Directors chair of the Edgar Allan Poe Foundation of Boston, Inc., Lewis worked with others to celebrate Poe in the city of his birth by having a square at the intersection of Boylston Street and Charles Street South dedicated to Poe in 2010 and then installing a statue of Poe in it in 2014. title: The Point of View Book Discussion Group: The Glass Hotel
description: [Central Library in Copley Square] We are a book group for adults that reads a wide variety of fiction and nonfiction. We meet the 3rd* Wednesday of every month at 2:30 p.m. at the Central Library in Copley Square and on Zoom. Our choice for December is The Glass Hotel by Emily St. John Mandel. Fiction. title: Boston Research Center Office Hours
description: [Central Library in Copley Square] The Boston Research Center (BRC) is a digital community history and archives lab that supports Boston residents in telling the stories of their neighborhoods and communities. Want help on your digital history project? Attend BRC Office Hours on the third Thursday of every month, in person at the BPL Central Library. BRC Office Hours are free and open to the public. No registration needed! Drop by the Mezzanine Conference Room 1 between 3 pm and 4:30 pm. How We Can Help: The Boston Research Center helps bring Boston’s deep neighborhood and community histories to light through the creation and use of new technologies. The BRC can support your ideas and projects in many different ways. This support may look like: Offering free introductory workshops about digital humanities tools and methodsSharing resources and toolkits to help demystify digital projects and community history workConsulting on project design and maintenance Connecting community historians with subject experts, research resources, and grant opportunitiesProviding technical support for digital history projectsHelping promote events centered on community projects If you aren't sure what you need, drop in! Our knowledgeable team members will be happy to assist you. Check out our projects to see our work. This program is organized by Boston Public Library's Community History Department. title: Handwriting the Constitution
description: [Central Library in Copley Square] Patrons and visitors are invited to handwrite the U.S. Constitution in Bates Hall at the Central Library in Copley Square. This program aims to create time and a quiet space to reflect and deepen one's understanding of this historic document. All supplies will be provided. Participants will first stop by the supply table outside of Bates Hall to pick up writing supplies and a copy of the Constitution, before proceeding to Bates Hall. Reproductions of John Adams's personal copy of the Constitution held by Special Collections will also be available to transcribe. This program is self-paced. Patrons are invited to stay for the whole session or simply stay as long as they would like. About Handwriting the Constitution Handwriting the Constitution is a social art project begun in 2017 by artist Morgan O'Hara. It invites people from all walks of life to meet in public spaces to handwrite the U.S. Constitution or other documents written to protect human rights and freedoms. This art practice was created so that people will know their rights, deepen their understanding of laws created to protect these rights, and to help resist negative thinking. The goal of this art practice is to encourage people to hold their own Handwriting sessions on a recurring basis; to create a physical and psychological space that explores the practice of concentrated writing as an art form, and a process designed to bring people together in a quiet and calming way, all by focusing on human rights. It has been identified as a powerful and transformative form of activism for introverts. Accessibility Notice: We strive to make our events accessible. To request a disability accommodation and/or language services, contact the department listed in the "Contact Info" pane on the right. Please allow at least two weeks to arrange accommodation. Programming at the Boston Public Library is funded through private support. To learn more about supporting the Library, please visit the Boston Public Library Fund's website.

title: Humanity of the Arts & Humanity of the Legal Services (Volunteer Lawyers for the Arts)
description: [Central Library in Copley Square] The internet is replete with legal information. Legal blogs, contract templates, statutes, cases and commentary, AI agents, etc. Why hire a lawyer when so many answers rest at your fingertips? Online resources can be helpful, but only if you can trust they’re legitimate. Even then, they don’t always reflect your specific legal needs or the unique challenges faced by your specific business. In this workshop, we’ll discuss some of the challenges with online and automated resources, and how to get the best bang for your buck working with a (human) lawyer!Accessibility Notice: We strive to make our events accessible. title: Intro to Contracts & Negotiation (Volunteer Lawyers for the Arts)
description: [Central Library in Copley Square] What is a contract? Are there things it must include? Do I need a lawyer to write or negotiate it for me? A contract exists when participants come together to exchange goods and services for compensation. A written contract is a valuable tool for any creative business. Contracts take all shapes and sizes, but the best contract is the one that all parties understand and that meets all parties’ business needs. Whether you routinely use contracts in your creative practice or you’re new to it, this workshop is for you! Accessibility Notice: We strive to make our events accessible. title: Copyright & Intellectual Property (Volunteer Lawyers for the Arts)
description: [Central Library in Copley Square] Copyright lasts a long time. For many creatives, the copyright on their works might last multiple lifetimes before it enters the public domain. This is why it’s so important for artists and creative workers to include copyright as part of their legacy plan. Who has the power to use, enjoy, publicize, and distribute your creative works?
